analysis.one_liner: Repeals the tax rules requiring reporting and withholding on offshore bank accounts.
analysis.headline: S. 869, a bill to repeal the offshore-account reporting and withholding rules known as FATCA, was introduced with 2 cosponsors in April 2017 and died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would erase the 2010 law (FATCA) that requires foreign banks to report accounts held by Americans, requires US taxpayers to disclose foreign financial assets over $50,000, and imposes penalties on people who hide foreign assets from the IRS. It would end withholding on payments to foreign institutions that don't comply, and strip out the added penalties for undeclared foreign accounts and foreign trusts. The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy Americans with money in foreign accounts, who would no longer face disclosure requirements or the extra penalties for hiding foreign assets. Foreign banks and financial institutions also benefit, because they would be freed from the cost of identifying and reporting their American account holders to the IRS. Americans living abroad would also gain, since they bear real paperwork burdens under the current rules even when they owe little or no US tax.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy offshore account holders and foreign banks

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the entire withholding regime for payments to foreign financial institutions and other foreign entities, ending the requirement that foreign banks identify US account holders or lose a share of US-source payments [S2][S3].

Eliminates the requirement that US taxpayers report foreign financial assets, and removes the extended six-year statute of limitations for large omissions of income connected to foreign assets [S2][S3].
Strikes the added penalty for underpaying tax attributable to undisclosed foreign financial assets, and removes the $10,000 minimum penalty for failing to report on certain foreign trusts [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The IRS and US taxpayers generally. The reporting regime is the main tool for detecting offshore tax evasion, so the bill would reduce federal revenue and shift more of the tax load onto people whose money is visible. Americans living abroad would be spared paperwork, but the cost of the repeal falls on honest domestic taxpayers whose liability would rise to cover what hidden offshore income no longer pays.
analysis.who_pays_short: The IRS and ordinary domestic taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The offshore reporting rules it repeals are the primary way the US government learns about American money hidden in foreign accounts; repealing them removes the disclosure requirements, the extended audit window, and the penalties that make evasion unprofitable [S2][S3].

The current rules do impose real costs on people who are not evading anything: banks in other countries have dropped American customers to avoid compliance costs, and Americans abroad file extensive reports even when they owe little US tax. The bill addresses that burden but does so by dismantling the entire enforcement structure rather than easing it for ordinary filers [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief for expatriates and foreign banks is real, but the bill's dominant effect is to remove disclosure and penalty rules that exist to catch hidden offshore income, and the savings to those parties would come at the expense of federal revenue and of taxpayers whose income is fully visible to the IRS.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent straight to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2017, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rand Paul introduced S. 869 on April 6, 2017, with Wicker as an original cosponsor, and it drew 2 cosponsors in total [S4][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced; no further action was ever recorded [S5].

The bill's stated purpose, in its own words, was to repeal 'the violation of sovereign nations' laws and privacy matters,' though its text consists entirely of repeals of US tax-reporting and withholding provisions on foreign accounts [S3].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with the bill still in committee, so every provision it would have repealed remained in force [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so the existing offshore-disclosure rules stayed in force. The IRS, the Treasury's enforcement of foreign-account reporting, and taxpayers whose income is visible to the government are better off than they would have been had the repeal passed. Americans living abroad continue to bear the reporting paperwork that motivated the bill.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: 1 additional Senate Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing the total to 2 cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no party split can be measured; the bill's entire sponsorship was Republican (the sponsor plus 2 cosponsors) [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill frees them from the cost of identifying and reporting American account holders, a compliance burden that has led some foreign banks to turn away US customers entirely. But the same reporting is how the US government detects offshore evasion, so removing it benefits the banks partly by taking away the transparency ordinary taxpayers rely on to keep the tax system fair.

Repeal would eliminate the disclosure requirement, the extended audit window, and the added penalties that apply specifically to undeclared foreign assets. Their gain would be paid for by domestic taxpayers whose income is fully reported.
